newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Futures--Dutch review moribund ATA wheat contract.
newsitem.headline: Futures--Dutch review moribund ATA wheat contract.

text.p: Amsterdam's Agricultural Futures Exchange (ATA) said on Thursday it had no plans to close down its fledgling European wheat futures contract, but was still studying proposals to change some of the specifications.
The contract has attracted little interest since its launch in the summer. On some days recently, turnover has been nil.
By mid-afternoon on Thursday, the market had drawn only one offer and had registered no volume.
"We have been carrying out an investigation with industry members and the trade to see what we can do to encourage more interest," ATA spokesman Robert Muller told Reuters.
He said the two main areas of focus would be the contract's quality specifications and the size of lots traded.
Muller said said some of the contract's quality restrictions might be relaxed to allow more bread-milling wheat from Europe's farmers on to the exchange.
"Maybe we will make a compromise in that area," Muller said.
The contract currently trades lots of 125 tonnes and this might be lowered to increase participation, he added. He could not say what precise lots sizes were being considered.
The investigation was still proceeding and a decision on possible changes was not expected until early 1997, he said.

The Europe-wide contract was launched in June at a time when speculative interest in the U.S. grain markets was high. Price fluctuations have calmed since and the ATA believes this is one factor behind their contract's poor performance.
"The main thing you need for success is a volatile cash market and we haven't had that recently," Muller said. "But we think that over the next 10 years this will be a volatile market."

A race to set up a European milling wheat contract to cash in on the speculative interest developed between the ATA and France's MATIF, with the Dutch exchange stealing a month's head start on its rival.
In the early stages the ATA said the rush to get the contract off the ground might have been part of the problem, blaming the timing -- between harvests -- for the sparse interest.
The MATIF contract has also struggled to attract volume, often trading well under 50 lots a day. On the French exchange, each contract is worth 50 tonnes.
MATIF officials were reluctant to set a turnover target but privately admitted that 1,000 contracts a day within two years would be a measure of success.
